text:
**Lisbon, Thu May 20 – Sun May 23**

I've assumed you take the overnight nonstop out of Boston on the evening of **Wed May 19**, land the morning of the 20th, and fly home on the 23rd. That's three hotel nights. If you meant leaving Boston on the 20th, tell me and I'll tighten the plan. A Thursday-to-Sunday trip also avoids the Monday closures at most Lisbon museums.

**Where to stay:** Baixa, Chiado, or the lower edge of Alfama. Everything below is walkable from there or a short Uber away. Skip Bairro Alto, which is the bar district and stays loud until 2 a.m. Aim for about €125/night for a good guesthouse or 3-star, and book soon, because late May fills up.

### Day 1 (Thu): Arrive, Baixa and Alfama
This day is kept light so you can get through the jet lag.
- Land around 8–9 a.m., take an Uber or Bolt to the hotel (~20 min, ~€15), and drop your bags.
- Have coffee and a pastel de nata at **Confeitaria Nacional**, which has been baking since 1829.
- Walk the Baixa from Rossio down Rua Augusta to the arch (take the lift up for the view) and out to Praça do Comércio. The whole street grid was rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake, tsunami, and fire. It was one of the first districts anywhere designed to survive the next quake.
- Back near Rossio, have a shot of ginjinha (sour-cherry liqueur) at **A Ginjinha**, a standing-room counter that has served it since 1840.
- Lunch: a bifana (garlicky pork sandwich) and a beer.
- Check in and nap, but keep it under 90 minutes.
- Around 5 p.m., take an Uber up to **Castelo de São Jorge**, the Moorish fortress that Portugal's first king captured in 1147. Then walk *down* through Alfama's lanes past Miradouro de Santa Luzia and Portas do Sol to the **Sé Cathedral**, which was begun the same year.
- Dinner: something early and simple at a small Alfama tasca, like grilled fish and a jug of vinho verde. Then go to bed.

### Day 2 (Fri): Sintra
Go to Sintra on a weekday, because it gets mobbed on Saturdays.
- Take a train around 8:30 from **Rossio station**, which is a neo-Manueline beauty itself. The ride is about 40 minutes.
- **Pena Palace:** book a 10:00 timed entry online in advance. Afterward, walk through the park to the **Moorish Castle**, whose walls run along the ridge.
- Take bus 434 or an Uber down to the old town for lunch. Then get **travesseiros and queijadas at Piriquita**, which has been open since 1862.
- In the afternoon, pick one of two:
  - The **National Palace** is a medieval royal palace with extraordinary tilework. It's the better pick for history lovers.
  - **Quinta da Regaleira** is an eccentric 1900s estate with a spiral "initiation well."
- Take the train back around 5.
- Dinner: **Cervejaria Ramiro**, the city's classic seafood restaurant. It doesn't take reservations, so arrive by 7 (locals eat around 9). Order the garlic prawns and clams Bulhão Pato, and finish with a *prego* (steak sandwich), the way locals do.

### Day 3 (Sat): Belém and Chiado
- Take the train from Cais do Sodré to Belém (~10 min). Be at **Jerónimos Monastery** when it opens, with tickets bought online. It's a Manueline masterpiece built with spice-trade money, and Vasco da Gama is buried there.
- Next door is **Pastéis de Belém**, the original custard-tart bakery (1837), which uses the monks' recipe. Skip the takeaway line and sit inside, where tables turn over fast.
- Walk along the waterfront to the **Monument to the Discoveries** and **Belém Tower**. The tower is best seen from outside; the line to go in usually isn't worth it on a short trip.
- Take the train back and have lunch at **Time Out Market**, right across from the station. It's touristy, but it's a quick way to try a lot of things.
- Spend the afternoon in Chiado:
  - Visit the **Carmo Convent**, a Gothic church that has stood roofless since 1755.
  - Do a nata taste-off at **Manteigaria** against the morning's Belém tart.
  - Stop at **Conserveira de Lisboa** (since 1930) for tinned fish to bring home.
- Farewell dinner: fado in Alfama. **Mesa de Frades**, set in an old tiled chapel, is a lovely choice. Book ahead. This is the trip's one splurge.

### Day 4 (Sun): Home
Flights from Lisbon to Boston usually leave late morning or midday. Get to the airport 3 hours early, because passport control at Lisbon's airport is notoriously slow. If your flight is in the afternoon, the **National Tile Museum** (opens at 10) is worth the detour. It covers 500 years of azulejos in a 1509 convent and includes a huge tile panorama of Lisbon before the earthquake.

### Budget (for two)
| | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Flights, Boston–Lisbon round trip (~$700 each) | $1,400 |
| Hotel, 3 nights (~€125/night + city tax) | $450 |
| Food and drink | $470 |
| Sights and tickets | $200 |
| Local transport (airport rides, trains, metro) | $80 |
| **Total** | **$2,600** |

That lands right at your budget with nothing to spare, and **flights are the big unknown**. Late-May fares from Boston can run from about $600 to over $900 per person. Set a fare alert now and book if you see $700 or less. Also check Azores Airlines, which connects through Ponta Delgada and is often cheaper than TAP's nonstop.

If fares come in high, here's where to make room:
- Stay in a guesthouse at about €100/night (saves ~$100).
- Hear fado at a small tasca instead of a dinner house (~$80).
- See only Pena plus one other site in Sintra (~$30).

### Good to know
- **Shoes:** Lisbon is steep hills and slick limestone cobbles, so wear shoes with good grip.
- **Weather:** late May is usually mid-70s and sunny. Sintra is cooler and often misty, so bring a layer.
- **Couvert:** the bread, olives, and cheese put on your table aren't free. You can eat them or send them back; either is completely normal.
- **Cheap, great lunches:** look for *prato do dia* (dish of the day) chalked up outside tascas, usually €10–14.
- **Getting around:** buy a Viva Viagem card at any metro station and load it with "zapping" credit. It works on the metro, trams, buses, and the Sintra and Belém trains. Skip Tram 28, which has long queues and is a favorite of pickpockets.
- **Book ahead:** Jerónimos, Pena Palace, and the fado dinner.
- **Paperwork:** check whether the EU's ETIAS travel authorization is required by May. It was scheduled to launch in late 2026, costs about €20 per person, and you apply online. The EU's new entry system also takes fingerprints and photos of first-time arrivals, so expect a line at passport control when you land.

Want me to suggest a few specific hotels in that price range?

Sure. One area per day leaves room for three areas, so something has to go. I'd drop **Sintra**. It's the longest, hilliest day of the trip, and Lisbon itself has plenty of history and food to fill your time. There's a way to swap it back in at the bottom if it's a must.

The earlier hotel area, booking-ahead advice, and tips all still apply.

### Day 1 (Thu): Baixa and Chiado
If you stay centrally, this is your own neighborhood, so there's almost no getting around to do on a jet-lagged day.
- **Morning:** Land, drop your bags, and have coffee and a nata at **Confeitaria Nacional**. Wander from Rossio down Rua Augusta to Praça do Comércio at whatever pace feels right.
- **Lunch:** A bifana and a beer. Then check in and nap.
- **Late afternoon:** Walk up to the **Carmo Convent** ruins, then have a nata at **Manteigaria** nearby.
- **Evening:** Have a ginjinha at **A Ginjinha**, then dinner at **Cervejaria Trindade**, the old beer hall in a former convent.

### Day 2 (Fri): Belém
- **Morning:** Take the train from Cais do Sodré and be at **Jerónimos Monastery** when it opens. Give the cloister real time. Afterward, go to **Pastéis de Belém** next door and sit inside.
- **Midday:** Stroll the riverfront to the **Monument to the Discoveries** and **Belém Tower**. The outside is the highlight, so there's no need to queue to go in.
- **Afternoon:** Take the train back and have a late lunch at **Time Out Market**, across from the station. The rest of the afternoon is free.
- **Evening:** Seafood at **Cervejaria Ramiro**. It doesn't take reservations, so arrive by 7.

### Day 3 (Sat): Alfama
- **Morning:** Take an Uber up to **Castelo de São Jorge** at 9, before the crowds. Then walk down to the **Portas do Sol** and **Santa Luzia** viewpoints.
- **Late morning:** Saturday is a market day at **Feira da Ladra**, the flea market just past the viewpoints. If you want one more sight, **São Vicente de Fora** next door has cloisters lined with tiles.
- **Lunch:** A long one at a tasca. Order the *prato do dia* (dish of the day).
- **Afternoon:** Drift downhill through the lanes to the **Sé Cathedral**, then go back to the hotel to rest.
- **Evening:** A farewell fado dinner at **Mesa de Frades**. Book ahead.

### Day 4 (Sun): Home
Same as before: get to the airport 3 hours early. If your flight is in the afternoon, the **National Tile Museum** makes an easy last stop.

**Budget:** Cutting Sintra saves about $100 on tickets and trains. With flights at about $700 each, that puts you around $2,500 total, so you'd have a small cushion.

**If Sintra is a must:** Swap it in for Belém on Friday. You'd lose Belém and the original custard tarts. Limit Sintra to Pena Palace in the morning, lunch in town, and the National Palace in the afternoon, and it stays fairly relaxed.

For this trip, I'd skip it, though it's a closer call than "skip" makes it sound.

**What Sintra has that Lisbon doesn't:** a forested ridge with a Moorish castle, Portugal's best-preserved medieval royal palace, and Pena, the brightly painted hilltop palace on every Portugal postcard. For history lovers, it's one of the great day trips in Europe.

**Why I'd still pass this time:**
- **It takes a third of your sightseeing time.** You have about two and a half usable days. A Sintra day also loses a couple of hours to trains, buses, and queues.
- **It's the opposite of the pace you asked for.** Pena is one of Portugal's most-visited sites. Even with a timed ticket, the inside is a slow shuffle through crowds, and the hills are steep. The hilltop can also be fogged in while Lisbon is sunny.
- **The food is weaker.** Sintra's highlight is its pastries. Lisbon is where the real eating is.
- **The history overlaps.** In Lisbon you already get a Moorish castle, a medieval cathedral, and a royal monastery.

**Go anyway if** the palaces are a big part of why you picked Portugal and you'd regret only ever seeing Pena in photos. In that case:
- Go on Friday, and give up the **Alfama** day rather than Belém. That changes what I suggested before. Sintra covers the castle-and-medieval history, and Alfama is close enough to your hotel to see at sunset before Saturday's fado dinner. Nothing replaces Belém, with Jerónimos and the original custard tarts.
- Limit it to two sites: Pena in the morning, lunch and pastries from Piriquita in town, and the National Palace in the afternoon.
- The cost is roughly the same, about $50 more than the all-Lisbon plan, because you'd skip the castle ticket.

The only way to do both without rushing is to add a fourth night. That would put you about $300 over budget.

This is the all-Lisbon version, without Sintra.

| Day | Area | Plan | Rough cost (for two) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Thu May 20** | Baixa & Chiado | **Morning:** Land, coffee and a nata at Confeitaria Nacional, then a stroll from Rossio to Praça do Comércio. **Afternoon:** Bifana lunch, nap, Carmo Convent, and a nata at Manteigaria. **Evening:** Ginjinha, then dinner at Cervejaria Trindade. | $130 |
| **Fri May 21** | Belém | **Morning:** Jerónimos Monastery at opening, then Pastéis de Belém. **Afternoon:** Walk along the river to the Discoveries Monument and Belém Tower, have a late lunch at Time Out Market, and take some free time. **Evening:** Seafood at Cervejaria Ramiro. | $235 |
| **Sat May 22** | Alfama | **Morning:** Castelo de São Jorge at 9, the viewpoints, and the Feira da Ladra flea market. **Afternoon:** Tasca lunch, a wander down to the Sé, and rest. **Evening:** Fado dinner at Mesa de Frades. | $235 |
| **Sun May 23** | Home | Breakfast, then head to the airport 3 hours before your flight. If your flight is in the afternoon, visit the Tile Museum first. | $40 |
| **Flights** | — | Boston–Lisbon round trip, ~$700 each | $1,400 |
| **Hotel** | Baixa/Chiado | 3 nights at ~€125/night, plus city tax | $450 |
| **Total** | | | **~$2,490** |

Each day's cost covers food, tickets, and local transport. The two big meals are Ramiro (~$105) and the fado dinner (~$135).

That leaves about **$110 of cushion**. Flights are still the number to watch: every $50 above $700 per ticket adds $100 to the total. Fares up to about $750 each still fit.

If you'd rather include Sintra, I can redo the table with that swap.

Honestly, you're cutting it close.

On paper you're about $110 under budget, which is roughly 4%. A comfortable cushion is more like 10–15%, or $250–400 on a $2,600 trip. Two things make it tighter than it looks:

**1. Flights decide everything.** The table assumes about $700 per ticket. At $850 each, you're $300 over before you land.

**2. Some costs aren't in the table:**
- **Getting to and from Logan:** $0–150, depending on whether you take the T, use Logan Express, ride in an Uber, or park.
- **Phone data:** carrier day passes can add up to about $100 for the two of you over four days. An eSIM costs around $10–20.
- **ETIAS,** if it's required by May: about $45 for two.
- **Extras:** souvenirs, extra coffees, and a bottle of port to bring home can easily add $50–100. Exchange-rate moves can also shift your euro costs by $50 either way.

Realistically, the plan as written lands somewhere around **$2,600–2,750**.

**To make it comfortable without changing the trip's character:**
- **Lock in flights at $700 or less each.** Set fare alerts now and book when you see a good fare. Everything else depends on this.
- **Book a hotel at about €100/night instead of €125.** That saves about $90, and decent guesthouses are still findable at that price if you book early.
- **Hear fado at a small tasca instead of Mesa de Frades.** That saves about $80, and amateur fado in a neighborhood tasca is arguably the more authentic version anyway.
- **Use an eSIM** instead of your carrier's day pass.
- Optional: take the metro from the airport instead of an Uber, which saves about $25.

With the hotel and fado changes, your cushion grows to about $280, which is enough to absorb the extras and still finish under $2,600.

If $2,600 is a hard ceiling, I'd make those changes now. If going $100–200 over wouldn't hurt, the plan is fine as it is.

**Day 1 (Thu): Baixa & Chiado, rainy version**

It's the same area, just moved indoors. No walk between stops takes more than about 10 minutes. The Carmo Convent is out because it's roofless.

- **Morning:** Land, drop your bags, and settle into **Confeitaria Nacional** for coffee and natas while you wait out the rain. Then head to the **Lisbon Story Centre** on Praça do Comércio, which takes about an hour. It's a walk-through history of the city with an immersive room on the 1755 earthquake, and it makes a good primer for the rest of the trip. The square's covered arcades will keep you dry on the way.
- **Lunch:** Have a bifana at a café counter near Rossio. Then get a ginjinha at **A Ginjinha** around the corner, which only takes two minutes, rain or not.
- **Afternoon:**
  - Check in and nap, still for under 90 minutes.
  - Instead of climbing wet hills, ride the long escalators inside **Baixa-Chiado metro station** up to Chiado.
  - Browse **Livraria Bertrand**, the world's oldest operating bookshop (1732), then have a warm nata at **Manteigaria**.
  - Finish at **São Roque church**. It's plain outside and astonishing inside, with a gilded chapel that was built in Rome and shipped to Lisbon in the 1740s.
- **Evening:** Have dinner at **Cervejaria Trindade** as planned. It's a two-minute walk from São Roque. If the rain stops before dinner, the Carmo ruins are just around the corner.

**Rain notes:** Lisbon's limestone cobbles get as slick as ice when wet, so wear shoes with real grip. Ubers get pricier in the rain, so use the metro when you can.

The cost is about the same as the dry version. The Story Centre ticket replaces Carmo's, and São Roque is free to enter.

Good news: Portuguese cooking relies much more on salt cod, pork, and bread than on shellfish, so you'll still eat very well.

The one change to your plan is **Friday's dinner**. Ramiro is built around shellfish, so swap it for **Taberna da Rua das Flores** in Chiado. It's a small tasca with a chalkboard menu of Portuguese small plates. It fills up, so go early. It's also a bit cheaper.

### What to look for

**Fish**
- **Bacalhau (salt cod):** the national obsession. Try **bacalhau à Brás**, a Lisbon original of shredded cod with eggs, onions, and matchstick potatoes. Also look for **pastéis de bacalhau** (cod croquettes) and **pataniscas** (cod fritters).
- **Grilled whole fish:** sea bream (*dourada*), sea bass (*robalo*), or horse mackerel (*carapau*) off a charcoal grill, with boiled potatoes and olive oil. It's the classic tasca lunch.
- **Sardines:** the season usually starts in June, so you might catch the first ones.
- **Tinned fish:** sardines, mackerel, and tuna. Read the labels, because many tins are mussels, clams, or octopus.

**Meat**
- **Secretos de porco preto:** a juicy grilled cut of Alentejo black pork.
- **Frango piri-piri:** chicken grilled with chili, cheap and great.
- **Alheira:** a garlicky sausage with a backstory for history fans. The story goes that Jewish converts invented it during the Inquisition, making it from poultry and bread so it would pass for pork sausage.
- **Chouriço assado:** chorizo flamed at your table in a clay dish.
- **Bifana** and **prego**, the pork and steak sandwiches, are already in your plan.

**Everything else**
- **Caldo verde:** kale and potato soup with a slice of chouriço.
- **Cheese:** Serra da Estrela or Azeitão, two soft sheep's-milk cheeses so ripe you eat them with a spoon.
- **Convent sweets:** egg-yolk desserts from convents and monasteries, which used the egg whites to starch clothes. The pastel de nata is one of them.

### Watch out for
- **Carne de porco à alentejana:** the name sounds like a pork dish, but it's pork *with clams*. This is the big trap.
- **Cataplana**, **caldeirada** (fish stew), and fish soups often include clams or mussels.
- Anything ***de marisco*** ("with shellfish"), such as arroz de marisco or açorda de marisco.
- **Rissóis de camarão:** shrimp turnovers that look just like the meat ones in pastry-shop display cases.
- **Octopus, squid, and cuttlefish** (*polvo, lulas, choco*) usually don't count as *marisco* in Portugal. If you avoid those too, name them specifically.

**Handy phrase:** *"Não comemos marisco"* means "we don't eat shellfish." If it's an allergy, say *"Sou alérgico/a a marisco"* instead, because grills and fryers are often shared. Most servers in Lisbon speak English, but it's worth saying either way. Mention it when you book the fado dinner, too.

**Lisbon, Thu May 20 – Sun May 23: 3 nights for two, $2,600 total**

**Sintra is out.** I recommended skipping it to keep the pace relaxed, and we've been working from the all-Lisbon plan since. If you change your mind, the swap would be Sintra on Friday in place of the Alfama day, with Belém moving to Saturday.

**What's settled**
- **Flights:** Take the overnight flight from Boston on Wed May 19, land the morning of the 20th, and fly home Sunday the 23rd.
- **Where to stay:** Baixa or Chiado, around €125/night. Avoid Bairro Alto, the nightlife district.
- **Pace:** One main area per day.
- **Food:** No shellfish. Ramiro is out and Taberna da Rua das Flores is in. Watch out for *carne de porco à alentejana* (pork with clams), cataplana, anything *de marisco*, and shrimp rissóis.

**The plan**
- **Thu (Baixa & Chiado):** Arrive, have natas at Confeitaria Nacional, stroll to Praça do Comércio, and nap. Then visit Carmo Convent, have a ginjinha, and eat dinner at Cervejaria Trindade.
  - *If it rains:* Lisbon Story Centre, the Bertrand bookshop, and São Roque church instead.
- **Fri (Belém):** Visit Jerónimos at opening, then Pastéis de Belém and the riverfront monuments. Have a late lunch at Time Out Market and dinner at Taberna da Rua das Flores.
- **Sat (Alfama):** See the castle at 9, then the viewpoints and the Feira da Ladra flea market. Have lunch at a tasca, walk down to the Sé, and end with a fado dinner.
- **Sun:** Get to the airport 3 hours early. If you fly in the afternoon, visit the Tile Museum first.

**Budget:** About $2,460 on paper, assuming flights cost around $700 each. That's tight. Extras not in the estimate, like getting to Logan, phone data, and souvenirs, could bring you to around $2,600 or slightly over.

**Still your call**
- **Is $2,600 a hard cap?** If so, book a hotel at about €100/night and hear fado at a small tasca instead of Mesa de Frades. Together, those changes free up about $170.

**To book or check**
- Set fare alerts now, and book flights at $700 or less each.
- Book the hotel, Jerónimos tickets, and the fado dinner. Mention no shellfish when you reserve.
- Check whether ETIAS is required by May, and get an eSIM.

Great place to start, because DNS happens *before* your browser sends that request you already know about.

## The problem DNS solves

Computers on the internet don't find each other by name. They use **IP addresses**: numbers like `142.250.80.46`. Think of them like phone numbers. They're what the network actually uses to route traffic to the right machine.

Humans, though, want to type `google.com`, not a string of numbers. So something has to translate names into addresses. That's **DNS**, the **Domain Name System**. It's essentially the internet's phone book.

So when you type a URL, the real sequence is:

1. **Look up the name**: "what's the IP address for `google.com`?" (DNS)
2. **Connect to that IP** and send the HTTP request (the part you already know)

## Why it's not one big phone book

You could imagine a single server holding a list of every domain and its IP. That would be a disaster:

- There are hundreds of millions of domains, constantly changing.
- Billions of devices doing lookups would crush it.
- If it went down, the whole internet would effectively go down.

So DNS is **split up and hierarchical**. No single server knows everything. Each one is responsible for its own slice and knows who's in charge of the slices below it.

## Domain names are a hierarchy (read right to left)

Take `www.example.com` and read it backwards:

```
.  (root)            ← the top of the tree, usually invisible
└── com              ← top-level domain (TLD)
    └── example      ← the domain someone registered
        └── www      ← a specific name within that domain
```

Each level is run by different people:

- **Root servers** know where the servers for every TLD (`.com`, `.org`, `.uk`, `.io`, …) are.
- **TLD servers** know which servers are in charge of each domain under them, like `example.com`. (The `.com` servers are run by a company called Verisign.)
- **Authoritative servers** for `example.com` hold the actual answers, like "`www.example.com` is at such-and-such IP." Whoever owns the domain picks these, and they're often run by the registrar or a provider like Cloudflare or AWS.

The key idea: **most servers don't know the final answer. They just know who to ask next.** This is called *delegation*.

## Who's involved in a lookup

- **Your computer.** Your operating system has a tiny DNS client that doesn't do the hard work. It just hands the question off to…
- **A recursive resolver.** This is the workhorse. It's usually run by your internet provider, or it's a public one like Google's (`8.8.8.8`) or Cloudflare's (`1.1.1.1`). It takes your question and chases down the answer for you.
- **Root, TLD, and authoritative servers.** The hierarchy above, which the resolver walks through.

## A lookup, step by step

Say you type `www.example.com` and nothing has been looked up recently (the IP addresses here are made up):

1. **Your browser → your OS:** "What's the IP for `www.example.com`?"
2. **Your OS → the recursive resolver:** same question.
3. **Resolver → a root server:** "Where's `www.example.com`?"
   → "No idea, but here are the `.com` servers. Ask them."
4. **Resolver → a `.com` server:** "Where's `www.example.com`?"
   → "No idea, but `example.com` is handled by `ns1.example-dns.net`. Ask them."
5. **Resolver → `ns1.example-dns.net`:** "Where's `www.example.com`?"
   → "It's `203.0.113.10`." ✅
6. **Resolver → your OS → your browser:** "`203.0.113.10`."
7. Your browser now connects to `203.0.113.10` and sends its HTTP request.

```
You ──► Recursive resolver ──► Root            "ask .com"
                           ──► .com server     "ask ns1.example-dns.net"
                           ──► Authoritative   "203.0.113.10"
You ◄── Recursive resolver
```

There are two styles of asking here. Your computer asks the resolver to **go get the final answer** (a *recursive* query). The resolver asks the other servers one step at a time and gets **referrals** back (*iterative* queries).

## Caching: why this is actually fast

That's several round trips across the world, which sounds slow. In practice most lookups are answered almost instantly, because **answers get cached everywhere**: in your browser, in your OS, and especially at the recursive resolver, which is shared by a huge number of people. Someone else on your ISP probably looked up `google.com` seconds ago, so the resolver already has the answer. The resolver also rarely needs the root servers at all, because it remembers where the `.com` servers are.

How long can something be cached? Every DNS answer comes with a **TTL (time to live)**, a number of seconds set by the domain's owner. A TTL of `3600` means "you can reuse this answer for an hour before asking again."

That's also why people say DNS changes "take time to propagate." Nothing is really spreading. Old cached copies around the world just have to expire.

## Records: what's actually stored

The authoritative server holds **records**. Each one has a name, a type, a value, and a TTL. The common types:

| Type | What it says | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | name → IPv4 address | `example.com → 203.0.113.10` |
| **AAAA** | name → IPv6 address (the newer, longer kind) | `example.com → 2001:db8::10` |
| **CNAME** | this name is an alias for another name | `www.example.com → example.com` |
| **MX** | where email for this domain should go | `example.com → mail.example.com` |
| **NS** | which servers are authoritative for this domain | `example.com → ns1.example-dns.net` |
| **TXT** | free-form text, often for verification and email security | `"v=spf1 ..."` |

When your browser looks up a website, it's asking for the **A** and/or **AAAA** records. The **NS** records are the "ask them next" pointers that make the step-by-step walk work.

## How a domain gets plugged in

When someone registers `mycoolsite.com`:

1. They buy it through a **registrar** (Namecheap, GoDaddy, Cloudflare, etc.).
2. The registrar tells the `.com` operator: "the authoritative servers for `mycoolsite.com` are X and Y." That's an NS record added one level up.
3. They put their actual records (A, MX, etc.) on servers X and Y.

Now the chain is connected: root → `.com` → their servers → the answer.

## Try it yourself

From a terminal on Mac or Linux (`nslookup` also works on Windows):

```bash
nslookup example.com      # simple lookup
dig example.com           # more detail, including the TTL
dig +trace example.com    # walk root → .com → authoritative, step by step
```

`dig +trace` is the fun one. It makes `dig` do the walk itself, starting at the root, and prints every referral. It's the walkthrough above, happening live.

## The one-sentence version

DNS turns names into IP addresses by walking a hierarchy (root, then TLD, then the domain's own authoritative servers, each of which only knows who to ask next), with caching at every layer so most lookups never need the full trip.

Want to go deeper on anything? Good next topics are what happens when DNS goes wrong, how CNAMEs and CDNs work together, or how DNS is secured.

Here's the same system told as a mail problem. The real terms are in **bold** as they come up, and there's a cheat sheet at the end.

## The setup

You want to mail a letter to a friend. You know their **name**, but the post office can't deliver to a name. It needs a **street address**.

- The name is the **domain name**: `www.example.com`
- The street address is the **IP address**: `203.0.113.10` (made up)
- The letter is your browser's **HTTP request**

**DNS** is the process of looking up the street address so the letter can go out. Your browser can't send anything until it has one.

## Step 1: Check your own address book

Before asking anyone, you flip through your own address book. Your computer does the same. The browser checks its **browser cache**, then the operating system checks its **OS cache** and the **hosts file** (think of a handwritten list taped inside the cover that takes priority over everything else).

If the address is there, you're done. Most of the time, it is.

## Step 2: Call the librarian

If it's not in your book, you don't go hunting yourself. You call a reference librarian and say, "Find me the address for `www.example.com` and call me back with the answer."

- The part of your computer that makes this call is the **stub resolver**. It doesn't do research. It just asks.
- The librarian is the **recursive resolver**. It's usually run by your internet provider, or it's a public one like Google's `8.8.8.8` or Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1`.
- "Go find it and bring me the final answer" is a **recursive query**.

## Step 3: The librarian works through a chain of directories

There's no single phone book for the whole world. The name is read **right to left**, from broadest to most specific (`com` → `example` → `www`), and there's a separate directory for each level. No directory has the whole answer. Each one just knows which directory to check next.

1. **The master index** = the **root servers**.
   "Names ending in `.com`? The `.com` directory office handles those. Here's where it is."
   An answer like "not me, ask them" is called a **referral**.

2. **The `.com` directory office** = the **TLD (top-level domain) servers**, run by Verisign for `.com`.
   "`example.com`? That family keeps its own address book at `ns1.example-dns.net`."
   That pointer is an **NS record**. Handing responsibility down a level like this is called **delegation**.

3. **The Example family's own address book** = the **authoritative name server**.
   It has the actual entry: "`www` lives at `203.0.113.10`."
   That entry is an **A record**. Because it comes from the official source, it's an **authoritative answer**.

The librarian asks each directory one step at a time and follows the referrals. Those step-by-step questions are **iterative queries**.

## Step 4: Mail the letter

The librarian calls you back with `203.0.113.10`. You write it on the envelope and send the letter. In real terms, your browser opens a connection to that IP and sends the HTTP request.

```
You ──"find www.example.com"──► Librarian (recursive resolver)
                                 ├──► Master index (root):            "ask the .com office"
                                 ├──► .com office (TLD):              "ask Example's own book"
                                 └──► Example's book (authoritative): "203.0.113.10"
You ◄──────"203.0.113.10"──────── Librarian
```

## The librarian's notepad (caching and TTL)

A good librarian writes down every answer, so the next person who asks gets it instantly. That's **caching**, and it's why DNS is fast. The librarian serves thousands of people, so popular addresses are almost always already on the notepad. She also remembers where the `.com` office is, so she rarely needs the master index.

But people move, so every entry in the family's address book comes with a "good for" stamp: "trust this for one hour, then check again." That's the **TTL (time to live)**, measured in seconds (`3600` = one hour).

This explains **DNS propagation**. When your friend moves, they update their own address book right away. But librarians everywhere still have the old address on their notepads until the "good for" time runs out. Nothing is actually spreading. Old copies are just expiring.

## What's in an address-book entry (record types)

The family's address book holds different kinds of entries, called **resource records**:

| Record | Address-book version | Real meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | "Lives at 203.0.113.10" | Name → IPv4 address |
| **AAAA** | Same, in the newer, longer address format | Name → IPv6 address |
| **CNAME** | "Bob? See the entry for Robert." | This name is an alias. Look up the other name instead. |
| **MX** | "Email for this household goes to the mailroom at…" | Which server accepts email for the domain |
| **NS** | "This family keeps its own address book at…" | Which servers are authoritative for the domain |
| **TXT** | The notes field | Free-form text, often used to prove ownership or for email security |

## Getting listed (registrars and registries)

When someone registers `mycoolsite.com`:

- The **registry** is the `.com` directory office itself (Verisign).
- The **registrar** (Namecheap, GoDaddy, Cloudflare, etc.) is the clerk you file the paperwork through.
- You tell the clerk where your address book lives: "my **name servers** are X and Y." The clerk gets that NS entry added at the `.com` office.
- Then you fill in your own address book on X and Y with your A, MX, and other records.

Now any librarian can find you: master index → `.com` office → your book → your address.

## Where the analogy breaks

- **One name can have several addresses.** Big sites list many IPs, like a chain store with many branches. The address book can even give a different branch depending on where you're asking from. That's a big part of how CDNs (content delivery networks) work.
- **Several names can share one address.** Think of many small businesses in one office building. One server can host thousands of websites.
- **It's fast.** The whole library trip, when it happens at all, takes a fraction of a second.

You're not wrong. In everyday use, that's exactly what people mean. When your Wi-Fi settings show a "DNS server," or someone tells you to "switch your DNS server to `1.1.1.1`," they're talking about the recursive resolver. I should have made that connection explicitly.

The catch is that **"DNS server" is an umbrella term**. Any server that answers DNS questions is a DNS server, and there are two very different kinds:

- **Recursive resolvers** look up answers *for you*. They don't own any records. Everything they know, they found out by asking around and then cached.
- **Authoritative servers** *hold* the records. They never go looking for anything. They just answer for the domains they're responsible for. Root servers, `.com` servers, and a domain's own name servers are all this kind.

In the analogy, the librarian is a DNS server, but so is every directory she visits. They just have different jobs.

| | Recursive resolver | Authoritative server |
|---|---|---|
| **Analogy** | The librarian | The directories and address books |
| **Who asks it** | Your devices | Recursive resolvers |
| **Where its answers come from** | Other servers (then its cache) | Its own records |
| **If it doesn't know** | Goes and finds out | Says "not mine" or refers you elsewhere |
| **Examples** | `8.8.8.8`, `1.1.1.1`, your ISP's resolver | Root servers, `.com` servers, Cloudflare or AWS Route 53 hosting a domain |
| **Other names you'll hear** | "DNS resolver," "recursive DNS server," "caching server," or just "DNS server" | "Name server," "authoritative DNS server" |

### Why the distinction matters

It shows up as two settings that sound alike but have nothing to do with each other:

- **"Change your DNS server to `1.1.1.1`"** (in your computer or router settings) changes which **resolver** *you* ask. It only affects your own lookups.
- **"Point your domain's nameservers to Cloudflare"** (at your registrar) changes which **authoritative servers** hold *your domain's* records. It affects everyone who looks up your domain.

Mixing those up is a really common mistake. In analogy terms, it's confusing "which library I use" with "where my family keeps its address book."

### One more wrinkle: your router

If you check your computer's network settings, the DNS server listed might be something like `192.168.1.1`. That's usually your home router acting as a **forwarder**: it takes your question and passes it along to the actual recursive resolver (typically your ISP's), often keeping a small cache of its own. Think of it as a front-desk receptionist who relays your request to the librarian.

One machine *can* play both roles. Company networks often have a server that's authoritative for internal names and also resolves everything else. But they're still two distinct jobs, and on the public internet they're usually kept separate.

| Server | What it does | What it typically says | Analogy | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Recursive resolver** | Does the lookup for you by asking the other three, then caches the result | "`www.example.com` is `203.0.113.10`" (the final answer) | The librarian | `8.8.8.8` (Google), `1.1.1.1` (Cloudflare), your ISP's resolver |
| **Root server** | Top of the hierarchy. Knows where each TLD's servers are | "Ask the `.com` servers" | The master index | `a.root-servers.net` through `m.root-servers.net` |
| **TLD server** | Knows which name servers handle each domain under its TLD | "Ask `example.com`'s name servers" | The `.com` directory office | Verisign's servers for `.com` |
| **Authoritative server** | Holds a domain's actual records (A, CNAME, MX, …) | "`www.example.com` is `203.0.113.10`" (the official answer) | The family's own address book | Cloudflare, AWS Route 53, or your registrar's name servers |

The resolver works down the last three rows in order (root → TLD → authoritative), skipping any step it already has cached.

One footnote: root and TLD servers are technically authoritative too, just for their own level of the hierarchy. When people say "authoritative server," they usually mean the domain's own name servers, as in the last row.

Let's follow it end to end. I'll pretend `meadowlark.example` is a real registered domain and that nothing is cached anywhere yet. (There's a real-world catch with `.example` that I'll get to at the end.) All the names and IP addresses below are made up.

### 1. The browser pulls out the name

You type `shop.meadowlark.example` and press Enter. The browser treats it as a web address and pulls out the **hostname**, `shop.meadowlark.example`. Before it can send anything, it needs that name's IP address.

### 2. Check the local address books

- **Browser cache:** "Have I looked this up recently?" No.
- **OS cache and hosts file:** The browser asks the operating system. The OS's **stub resolver** checks its own cache and the hosts file. Nothing there either.

### 3. Ask the recursive resolver

The stub resolver sends a **DNS query** (a small UDP packet to port 53) to whatever DNS server your settings point to, possibly by way of your router, which forwards it on. The query asks:

> What are the **A** records for `shop.meadowlark.example`?

It usually sends a matching query for **AAAA** (IPv6) records at the same time.

This is a **recursive query**: "get me the final answer." The resolver (the librarian) checks its cache, finds nothing, and starts the walk. Names are read right to left, so it starts at the top.

### 4. Root server: "ask the `.example` servers"

**Resolver → root server:** "A records for `shop.meadowlark.example`?"

The root (the master index) knows nothing about `meadowlark` or `shop`. It only knows about TLDs, so it sends back a **referral**:

> `.example` is handled by `a.nic.example` and `b.nic.example`. Here are their IP addresses.

The resolver caches this. Referrals from the root usually have long TTLs (often two days), so for a while the resolver can skip the root for anything ending in `.example`.

### 5. TLD server: "ask meadowlark's name servers"

**Resolver → `a.nic.example`:** same question.

The TLD server (the `.example` directory office) doesn't have `shop`'s address either. But it knows who's in charge of `meadowlark.example`, because the registrar filed that information when the domain was registered:

> `meadowlark.example` is handled by `ns1.meadowlark.example` (`198.51.100.53`) and `ns2.meadowlark.example` (`198.51.100.54`).

Those are the domain's **NS records**, which make up the **delegation**. Notice the chicken-and-egg problem here: the name servers live *inside* `meadowlark.example`, so normally you'd have to ask them for their own address. The TLD gets around this by including their IPs right in the referral. Those included addresses are called **glue records**.

The resolver caches this too.

### 6. Authoritative server: the actual answer

**Resolver → `ns1.meadowlark.example`:** "A records for `shop.meadowlark.example`?"

This server is **authoritative** for `meadowlark.example` (the family's own address book). It holds the domain's **zone**, meaning the full set of its records, and it finds the entry:

> `shop.meadowlark.example` → `203.0.113.25`, TTL 300

That's an **authoritative answer**. The TTL of 300 seconds means caches can reuse this answer for 5 minutes.

### 7. The answer travels back

The resolver caches the answer for 5 minutes and sends it back to your OS. The OS caches it and hands it to the browser, which caches it too.

### 8. The browser connects

DNS is done. Now the browser:

1. Opens a connection to `203.0.113.25` on port 443 (HTTPS).
2. Starts the encrypted TLS handshake, which includes the name `shop.meadowlark.example`. This is called **SNI** (Server Name Indication), and it tells the server which site's certificate to present.
3. Sends the HTTP request with the header `Host: shop.meadowlark.example`.

Steps 2 and 3 exist because many sites can share one IP address. The name you typed rides along so the server knows which site you want.

### The whole trip at a glance

```
Browser cache            ✗ miss
OS cache / hosts file    ✗ miss
Stub resolver ──► Recursive resolver (cache: miss)
                    ├─► Root:                    "ask a.nic.example"
                    ├─► .example TLD:            "ask ns1.meadowlark.example (198.51.100.53)"
                    └─► ns1.meadowlark.example:  "shop = 203.0.113.25, TTL 300"
              ◄── 203.0.113.25
Browser: connect to 203.0.113.25 → TLS → HTTP request
```

### What happens next time

- **You, two minutes later:** your browser or OS still has the answer cached. No DNS traffic at all.
- **Someone else using the same resolver, two minutes later:** the resolver answers straight from its cache.
- **Anyone, an hour later:** the 5-minute TTL has expired, but the resolver still remembers the root and TLD referrals, which usually last much longer. It skips straight to step 6 and asks `ns1.meadowlark.example` directly.

That's why the full walk from the root is rare in practice.

### The real-world catch

`.example` is a **reserved TLD**, set aside for documentation (like `example.com`). It has never been added to the root zone. So if you actually typed `shop.meadowlark.example` into a browser, the trip would end at step 4. The root would reply **NXDOMAIN** ("non-existent domain"), the resolver would pass that back, and with no IP address there'd be nothing to connect to. (Some browsers may not even try. If they don't recognize the ending as a real TLD, they might treat what you typed as a search instead.)

You can see the NXDOMAIN for yourself:

```bash
dig shop.meadowlark.example
```

Look for `status: NXDOMAIN` near the top of the output.

## Caching: remembering answers

Looking up a name from scratch takes several back-and-forth trips (root, then TLD, then the domain's own servers). Doing that every time you clicked a link would be slow, and it would bury those servers in traffic.

So everyone along the way **remembers answers** they've already gotten. That's all caching is. It happens in a few places:

- **Your browser** remembers names you've visited recently.
- **Your computer** keeps its own list, shared by all your apps.
- **The resolver** (the librarian) remembers answers for *everyone* who uses it. If anyone else asked recently, you get the answer instantly.

Most lookups get answered from one of those memories and never go any further.

## TTL: how long an answer can be remembered

The catch with remembering is that things change. A website might move to a new server, and old answers would send people to the wrong place.

So every answer comes with an expiration timer called the **TTL** (short for "time to live"). It's a number of seconds, chosen by whoever runs the domain:

- `300` = 5 minutes
- `3600` = 1 hour
- `86400` = 1 day

Think of it like the "use by" date on a carton of milk. Until then, you use what you have. After that, you throw it out and get a fresh answer.

One detail matters a lot: **the clock keeps running as the answer gets passed along.** If the resolver got an answer 4 minutes ago with a 5-minute TTL, it tells your computer "this is good for 1 more minute," not "5 minutes." So no matter how many places an answer gets copied to, every copy expires on the original schedule.

## The trade-off

Whoever runs a domain has to pick a TTL, and it's a balancing act:

| | Long TTL (say, 1 day) | Short TTL (say, 5 minutes) |
|---|---|---|
| **Lookups** | Fewer, so slightly faster for visitors | More frequent |
| **Load on the domain's servers** | Lighter | Heavier |
| **When you change something** | Some people may see the old answer for up to a day | Everyone sees the new answer within minutes |

Lots of sites land somewhere between 5 minutes and an hour. Things that almost never change, like which servers are in charge of a domain, often get a day or more.

## Why "DNS changes take time to spread"

When people say a change is "propagating," nothing is actually traveling around the internet. Each cache just holds on to the old answer until its timer runs out, and those timers run out at different moments. That's why some people see the change right away and others don't.

A common trick before a planned move: **lower the TTL ahead of time**, at least as far ahead as the old TTL (so if it's set to a day, do it a day early). The old, longer timer has to run out before the shorter one takes effect. Then make the change, and everyone picks it up within minutes. Once things settle, raise the TTL back up.

## "Doesn't exist" gets remembered too

If you look up a name *before* it's been created, the answer "no such name" gets remembered as well, for a while. So if you check a new address too early, then add it, then check again, you might keep getting "not found" for a bit. Nothing is broken. The "no" just hasn't expired yet.

## Two small caveats

- You can clear your own computer's memory of answers, but you can't make everyone else's caches forget early.
- Not every cache follows the timer perfectly. Some hold answers a little longer or shorter than they're told, so treat the TTL as "about how long," not a guarantee.

DoH changes **one leg of the trip**: how your question gets from your device to the recursive resolver. Everything else works the same, including the walk from root to TLD to authoritative server, the records, caching, and TTLs.

## The problem it solves

In the walkthrough, step 3 was your computer sending a small UDP packet to port 53. That packet isn't encrypted. In mail terms, it's a **postcard**. Anyone who handles it along the way can read it, and someone could even swap in a fake reply. That includes whoever runs the Wi-Fi you're on and your internet provider. Since you look up a name for almost every site you visit, those postcards add up to a pretty good record of your browsing.

## What DoH does

DNS over HTTPS puts the exact same question inside an **encrypted HTTPS connection**, the same kind your browser uses for secure websites. Now it's a **sealed envelope**. It also travels on port 443 mixed in with all your other web traffic, so it doesn't even stand out as DNS.

So step 3 changes from:

> UDP packet to `1.1.1.1`, port 53: "A records for `shop.meadowlark.example`?" (readable by anyone in between)

to:

> Encrypted HTTPS request to `https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query` carrying the same question (readable only by the resolver)

The question and answer inside are identical. Only the packaging changes.

## What it doesn't change

- **The resolver still sees everything.** The librarian has to open the envelope to answer it. DoH doesn't hide your lookups from the resolver. It means you're trusting *that* company instead of everyone on the network between you and it.
- **The resolver's own trips are still mostly postcards.** Its conversations with the root, TLD, and authoritative servers usually still use plain, unencrypted DNS. DoH protects the leg between you and the resolver, not the rest.
- **It doesn't prove the answer is genuine.** DoH stops tampering on the way to you, but if the resolver itself was handed a bad answer, DoH won't catch it. Checking that answers are authentic is a separate system called **DNSSEC**.
- **The site you connect to afterward can still leak.** Remember SNI from the walkthrough? The browser normally sends the site's name unencrypted during the TLS handshake, and the IP address you connect to can be a clue too. A newer feature called **Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)** closes the SNI gap, but it isn't used everywhere yet.

```
Browser ══ encrypted (DoH) ══► Recursive resolver
                                 ├── plain DNS ──► Root
                                 ├── plain DNS ──► .example TLD
                                 └── plain DNS ──► ns1.meadowlark.example
Browser ── connect + TLS (name visible via SNI unless ECH) ──► 203.0.113.25
```

## Who does it, and a side effect

Your operating system can do DoH, but often **the browser does it itself**. Firefox and Chrome both have it built in (look for a "DNS over HTTPS" or "secure DNS" setting). When the browser handles it, it may skip your computer's normal lookup process and talk straight to its chosen resolver.

That's mostly good, but it can cause surprises:

- Networks that rely on DNS for **filtering**, like parental controls or office security tools, can get bypassed.
- **Internal company names** that only the office's own DNS server knows about may stop working.

Browsers try to detect these situations and fall back to regular DNS, and companies often switch DoH off on work machines.

## Its sibling: DNS over TLS (DoT)

DoT does the same job (encrypting the trip to the resolver) but uses its own dedicated port, 853. That makes it easy for network operators to spot, manage, or block, whereas DoH blends in with ordinary web traffic. Android's "Private DNS" setting is built on DoT.

**In short:** DoH turns your DNS postcard into a sealed envelope for the trip to the resolver. It hides your lookups from the network, not from the resolver, and the rest of the process stays the same.

Here's the whole thing, start to finish, using `shop.meadowlark.example` as the example.

## The flow

1. **You type a name, but computers need a number.** Your browser can't connect to `shop.meadowlark.example` directly. First it needs the site's IP address, the way a letter needs a street address. DNS is the system that looks it up.

2. **Your browser and computer check their own memory first.** If you've been there recently, the address is already saved (cached), and the lookup is over before it starts.

3. **If not, your computer asks a resolver.** This is a server, usually run by your internet provider or a company like Google or Cloudflare, whose whole job is finding answers for you. It's what people usually mean by "your DNS server." It checks its own memory first too, and since it serves lots of people, it often already knows.

4. **If the resolver doesn't know, it works down from the top, reading the name right to left.**
   - It asks a **root server**, which says, "I don't know, but here's who handles `.example`."
   - It asks the **`.example` server**, which says, "I don't know, but here's who handles `meadowlark.example`."
   - It asks **`meadowlark.example`'s own server**, which actually has the answer: "`shop` is at `203.0.113.25`."

   Only the last server knows the final answer. The others just know who to ask next.

5. **The answer comes back with an expiration timer (the TTL).** The resolver, your computer, and your browser all save it until the timer runs out, so the next lookup is instant. The resolver also remembers who handles `.example` and `meadowlark.example`, so next time it can skip straight to the end.

6. **Your browser connects.** With the IP address in hand, the browser connects to that server, tells it which site it wants (since many sites can share one address), and loads the page.

## A few things that fit around that flow

- **There are two kinds of DNS servers.** Resolvers *look up* answers for you. Authoritative servers *hold* the answers for their own domains. Root and TLD servers count as authoritative too, just for the top levels.
- **Changes take time because of caching.** When a site changes its address, old copies stick around until their timers run out. Nothing is actually spreading. Old answers are just expiring. "That name doesn't exist" answers get remembered for a while too.
- **Regular DNS isn't private.** Your question to the resolver normally travels unencrypted, so people on your network can see what you look up. DNS over HTTPS encrypts that one leg. The resolver still sees your question, and the rest of the process is unchanged.
- **Domains get plugged in when they're registered.** The registrar tells the TLD which servers hold that domain's records. That's the link that makes step 4 work.

## The one-sentence version

Your browser needs an IP address for the name you typed, so it asks a resolver, which (unless it already remembers) follows a chain of servers from the top of the name down to the domain's own server, then hands the answer back to be remembered for as long as its timer allows.

Walk along the river past the Discoveries Monument to Belém Tower, which is better from outside than in. In the afternoon, see the Carmo Convent in Chiado, a Gothic church that lost its roof in the earthquake and was left that way, then walk up to the São Pedro de Alcântara viewpoint. Finish with a fado dinner in Alfama. It's a seated meal with singers performing between courses, so it suits a food trip, and you'll need a reservation.

Sunday: A last nata, then a taxi to the airport, about 20 minutes and €15-20. Flying home Monday instead would give you a full Sunday for about $300 more in hotel and meals, which the budget doesn't cover.

Rough budget for two:

- Flights: about $1,400, assuming TAP comes in around $700 each round trip
- Hotel: about $450 for three nights at $140, including Lisbon's tourist tax of €4 per person per night
- Food: about $500, with the fado dinner as the one big meal
- Sights and transport: about $250, mostly entry tickets in Sintra and Belém

That's the full $2,600, so the airfare decides whether this works. I haven't checked live fares; if TAP is high, also price Azores Airlines, which connects through Ponta Delgada. On the ground, the easiest savings are a guesthouse instead of a hotel and making lunch your main meal, since most tascas do a prato do dia for €10-15. The bread and olives brought to the table aren't free, so send them back if you don't want them.

Once flights are set, book the Pena Palace and Jerónimos time slots and the fado dinner.

Thursday: Alfama. Drop your bags, get a nata and an unhurried lunch near the hotel, then check in and sleep for a couple of hours. Around 5, take the 737 bus from Praça da Figueira up to Castelo de São Jorge, which stays open into the evening in May. Walk downhill from there through Alfama, past the Santa Luzia viewpoint to the Sé, and stay in the neighborhood for the fado dinner.

Friday: Sintra. Pena Palace in the morning on your booked time slot, then the bus back down to town for lunch and the National Palace. Pick up travesseiros at Casa Piriquita and be on a train back by mid-afternoon. Cervejaria Ramiro is two metro stops from Rossio, where the Sintra train comes in, so dinner there is easy after a rest at the hotel.

Saturday: Belém. Jerónimos Monastery when it opens, then custard tarts at Pastéis de Belém next door. Walk along the river to Belém Tower if you feel like it, then take the train back to Cais do Sodré for a late lunch at Time Out Market and have the afternoon off. For dinner, Taberna da Rua das Flores is a short walk from the hotel.

Sunday: A last nata and the airport.

This drops the Aljube museum, the Moorish Castle and the Carmo Convent, which saves about $50 in tickets and leaves you a little under the $2,600.

Yes, for the two of you I'd keep it. The National Palace in town is the best-preserved medieval royal palace in Portugal, and Pena is the 19th-century summer palace of the royal family, with the rooms kept as they were when the family left in 1910. The train is 40 minutes each way, so you're back for dinner and only give up the daytime.

Stay in Lisbon instead if you'd rather spend that day eating and wandering. Pena is crowded even on weekdays in May, and the food in Sintra is mostly pastries. If you drop it, I'd give Friday to the National Tile Museum, which is in a 16th-century convent with a gilded chapel, then a long lunch and a free afternoon.

Lots of the local classics have no shellfish in them:

- Bacalhau à Brás, salt cod scrambled with eggs, onions and thin fried potatoes, and pastéis de bacalhau, the cod fritters at most café counters
- Grilled sardines if they're in season yet (they usually come in around June), otherwise whole grilled dourada (sea bream) or robalo (sea bass)
- Bifanas, pork marinated in garlic and white wine on a roll, and pregos, the steak version
- Porco preto, the black Iberian pig from the Alentejo, usually grilled
- Arroz de pato, duck rice baked with slices of chouriço on top
- Frango piri-piri, grilled chicken brushed with chili oil
- Queijo da Serra, a soft sheep's-milk cheese you eat with a spoon, and presunto, cured ham
- Polvo à lagareiro, roasted octopus with potatoes and olive oil, if octopus is fine for you

Watch for carne de porco à alentejana. It sounds like a pork dish, but it's pork cooked with clams. Anything "de marisco" has shellfish, and caldeirada, the fish stew, sometimes has mussels. Telling the waiter "não comemos marisco" (we don't eat shellfish) covers it. If it's an allergy, use the word "alergia," and ask about octopus and squid too, since they're on most menus.

Ramiro is almost all shellfish, so I'd swap Friday's dinner for Casa do Alentejo, a few minutes' walk from Rossio station when you get back from Sintra. Order the porco preto or the migas there and skip the porco à alentejana. It's cheaper than Ramiro too, by about $35.
